title: The Bake-off
tagline: Which open-weight models can do real agent work on one consumer GPU, how fast, and with what settings.

hardware.weights: read over the network from a NAS, ~180-280 MB/s first load
hardware.agent: OpenCode 1.18 in a sandboxed container (some runs: Pi)

caveats: This is a living snapshot of the current state, not an apples-to-apples benchmark. The harness, prompts, grading, engines and client settings changed as we learned (see the timeline); results from different eras are not directly comparable.

n = 1 per row. One model swung 5/5, 5/5, 2/5 on identical settings; OrcaSAQ wrote a broken HTTP client once and a correct one the next time. A one- or two-check difference is noise. Read pass / partial / fail.

tok/s is generation throughput averaged over the whole agent run (output + reasoning tokens over wall time). It includes prompt processing, tool time and compaction, so it is lower than a short-prompt benchmark and depends on the task.
Settings were tuned per model (context, expert offload, KV type, thinking budget) to fill one RTX 3090. Each model ran at its own best fit, not at identical settings.
Uncensored models are tested for capability on our own software only; the tasks are the same coding tasks as for every other model.

tests.name: Command-line tool
tests.what: Write a Python CLI for the Home Assistant REST API.
tests.graded: The grader runs the tool in a sandbox: entry point and help, real data, bad input, bad token, no crash (5 checks), plus the model's own tests.

tests.name: MCP server in Rust
tests.what: Build a Model Context Protocol server in Rust from the spec on disk.
tests.graded: Built and driven as a real MCP client: initialize, tools/list and a tools/call that must return real data. Pass, partial or fail.

tests.name: Trust the docs
tests.what: Test 2 with a REST reference that has three planted wrong endpoints.
tests.graded: Did the model test, avoid, hedge or trust the planted endpoints? Read from the replay's access log and the shipped code.

tests.name: Use and fix an MCP server
tests.what: Describe a recorded house through an MCP server, then find and fix what is wrong with it.
tests.graded: Facts checked against the recording, a judgement on whether the server can be trusted, and the fix run against the client.

tests.name: Ticket fixes in Rust
tests.what: Fix three tickets in a known-good Rust MCP server.
tests.graded: Hidden black-box checks run against the built server, plus its 155 existing tests; a claim of 'done' that fails the checks is counted.

tests.name: Brass orrery
tests.what: One reply, no tools: an animated SVG orrery with planets at real ratios and a meshing gear train.
tests.graded: Rendered offline in a container with no network; five points of 0-2 (draws, planets, gears, lighting, motion).

tests.name: Voxel pagoda
tests.what: One reply, no tools: a three.js voxel Japanese pagoda with cherry trees, pond and torii.
tests.graded: Rendered offline with software WebGL; five points of 0-2 (draws, voxels, pagoda, setting, life).

tests.name: The labyrinth
tests.what: Write a seeded generator for a three-floor labyrinth meeting ten rules.
tests.graded: Ten unseen seeds, each in its own container, must give ten different mazes that pass the checker; walkability and honest notes are judged by hand.

tests.name: Pagoda and orrery as agent tasks
tests.what: Tests 5 and 6 solved by an agent with a sealed browser.
tests.graded: Same rubrics as tests 5 and 6, from offline renders of the file the agent leaves; two-hour cap.

tests.name: Surprising pagoda
tests.what: Build one pagoda page in steps: the scene, a surprise, then a trace of that surprise.
tests.graded: Two equal halves, each 0 to 10. Pagoda uses the test 6 scene criteria. Workflow is scored from the map: how the work was split and ordered, and whether it stopped for a person.

findings.title: Flash-Next at 500k to 1M total context: it fits and recalls, but no shape gives every session 40 tok/s yet
findings.summary: Alex's target is Flash-Next (UD-Q2_0) with 500k to 1M tokens in total across several sessions at about 40 tok/s each. Two active 256k sessions on the 3090 alone hold about 480k live tokens: both recalled their markers, 104.9 tok/s in total but split 55.0 and 35.0 per stream. Parking adds the rest: four ~248k sessions (about 1M kept) in a 28 GiB host-RAM cache all recalled correctly and came back in 1.30 s median, though the cache evicted 3 entries. Three active 256k sessions across both cards (about 720k live, power-capped) also fit and recalled, but split 18.8, 25.3 and 45.4 tok/s. In the same round Nemotron 3.5 Lightning reached 211.8 tok/s in total with four ~60k sessions, again unevenly (23.5-53.3 per session).

metrics.label: Slower of two active ~240k sessions, Flash-Next on the 3090 (short benchmark)
First token after switching back to a parked ~248k session, median
Slowest of three active ~240k sessions across both cards (short benchmark)

findings.quality: Marker recall only; no agent work graded on these shapes yet. Two OpenCode agents on the two-slot shape are queued.
findings.caveat: Short benchmarks, one run each, cards power-capped until a bigger power supply is in. A total rate divided by the session count is not a per-session rate.

findings.title: Four agents at once again: Cyber-Tiel-Coder passes both test 1 runs, Nemotron with thinking on passes test 2, and neither finishes the labyrinth inside the new time cap
findings.summary: Two more four-agent rounds on one load across both cards (OpenCode, tests 1, 2, 7 and test 1 again). Nemotron 3.5 Lightning Q8_0 with thinking on: test 2 builds, returns recorded data and passes its own 12 tests, but both test 1 runs miss most live checks, and the labyrinth agent was still looping after 22 hours, so it was stopped under Alex's new duration policy and scored 0 (its generator never finds a path). Cyber-Tiel-Coder 35B-A3B abliterated UD-Q6_K_XL with thinking off: both test 1 runs pass every live check (18 and 31 of their own tests), test 2 builds and passes 18 tests but its main read tool returns no recorded data, and the labyrinth agent was stopped automatically at the 3-hour cap having written a generator script but never the required ./generate program, so it scored 0. Agent-run rates: Cyber-Tiel sessions 28.9-35.2 tok/s each while four ran, the labyrinth about 95 tok/s per request once alone, first token median 6.6 s (Nemotron thinking on: 30.2-38.0 tok/s per session, first token median 0.59 s). Every session ran without a harness error.

metrics.label: Agent-run decode per session, Cyber-Tiel-Coder, four OpenCode agents at once (lowest)
Agent-run decode per session, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning thinking on, four at once (lowest)

findings.quality: Cyber-Tiel: 2 of 4 clean (both test 1); Nemotron thinking on: 1 of 4 clean (test 2). Both labyrinths 0/10 after a time stop.
findings.caveat: One run per shape. A clean harness finish is not proof of competence; the labyrinth results are graded as they stood at the stop.

findings.title: Flash-Next on the 3090 passes two OpenCode agents at once at 256k; a Cyber 27B fits four ~90k sessions on the V100 alone, slowly
findings.summary: Alex now wants two separate backends: a smart model on the 3090 with system RAM, and an uncensored Cyber model fully on the V100 with four sessions and as much context as practical. Smart lane: Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 on the 3090 alone (two 256k slots, 8-bit K/V, a 28 GiB session cache in host RAM, never disk) ran OpenCode test 1 and test 2 at the same time with thinking on. Test 1 passes all five live checks with 17 subcommands (our grader could not import its own test suite, so its tests are not counted); test 2 builds, exposes 9 tools, returns recorded data and passes 168 of its own tests. Both finished on their own inside the time caps: 64 and 71 minutes, 37.6 and 50.5 tok/s agent-run (48.1 and 57.3 tok/s decode), first token median 0.94 and 0.74 s, largest prompts about 189k and 217k tokens. A parked 189k-token session came back from host RAM with its first token in 0.89 s. Cyber lane, short benchmarks on the V100 alone: Qwen3.8-27B Cyber Q5_K_M fits four 64k slots (2.2 GiB free) and four 72k (1.0 GiB free) but not four 80k; the IQ4_XS quant fits four 96k slots (2.7 GiB free) and is faster (36.3 vs 28.6 tok/s on one session). With four long prompts the card reads them one at a time at about 400-490 tok/s, so the last of four ~90k prompts waits 14 minutes for its first token, and four sessions decode at about 8-9.5 tok/s each.

metrics.label: Agent-run decode per session, Flash-Next UD-Q2_0, two OpenCode agents at once on the 3090 (lowest)
Cyber 27B IQ4_XS on the V100, four ~90k sessions decoding at once (total)

findings.quality: Flash-Next: 2 of 2 clean (test 1 all live checks, test 2 with recorded data). Cyber 27B: quick quality check 3 of 3 and long-context recall correct on both quants; no agent tests yet.
findings.caveat: One run per shape. The two lanes were tested one at a time, not running together yet. Cyber four-session rates are short benchmarks, not agent runs.

findings.title: TensorFold 1.2.7 runs Qwen3.8-27B at 176k on one 3090 with lossless drafting
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates. The TensorFold 1.2.7 release, unchanged, now serves Qwen3.8-27B (EXL3 3-bit, DFlash2 drafter) on the 3090 with an 8-bit cache: 128k and 176k needle retrieval are correct (first token 249 s and 388 s), where the October build held 42k to 73k with its bf16-only cache and needed a local patch. Drafting gives 79-87 tok/s on prose, 210-217 on code and 204-259 on JSON, and the drafted replies match plain decoding on all 15 fixed prompts, greedy and sampled. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in NVFP4 also runs on the 3090's fallback path at 152-194 tok/s, but answered only 1 of 3 quality prompts correctly.

TensorFold code decode, plain against DFlash2 drafts

findings.quality: Qwen3.8-27B 3 of 3 on the quality check; Nemotron NVFP4 1 of 3.
findings.caveat: One run each, short benchmarks, no agent test yet. The October and November runs use different quants (4-bit then, 3-bit now).

findings.title: Arete-27B takes full marks on the labyrinth's A-C on the V100 alone; the V100 alone holds 240k for Arete and 2 x 256k for Flash-Next
findings.summary: Agent-run rates for the labyrinth, short-benchmark rates for the rest. Arete-27B Q6_K (a Nous Research fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B) on the V100 alone, thinking on, OpenCode: a working generator with 10 of 10 distinct hidden-seed mazes and the round trip, so full A-C marks, then D 1 (a comb-shaped maze with stairs bunched at both ends) and E 1 (its notes claim 65 distinct files from a list with one seed twice), 8 of 10 in 4.4 hours at 21.0 tok/s, first token median 0.61 s. It is the first dense 27B to reach full A-C marks, at about a sixth of Flash-Next's speed. On the same card alone Arete Q6_K fits up to 240k (235k retrieval correct, first token 15 min) and Q8_0 up to 128k; Tiel-Coder-35B Q6 fits 64k at 92 tok/s; and Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 on Strata holds two 256k sessions with all K/V on the card and 3.1 GiB spare, though it prefills one session at a time.

metrics.label: Arete-27B Q6_K largest working context on the V100 alone

findings.quality: Labyrinth A 2, B 2, C 2, D 1, E 1; every retrieval needle correct.
findings.caveat: One run each. The 256k Arete run retrieved correctly but missed our 512 MiB V100 floor by 72 MiB, so 240k is the published maximum.

findings.title: Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 holds eight ~240k sessions at once across our two cards; Unsloth's V3.1 Qwen3.8-27B file is the same speed as the old one
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates. Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 on Strata 0.2.13 across the 3090 and the V100, thinking on: with 20k K/V cells per layer on the cards and the rest in pinned host RAM, eight 256k slots took eight ~240k prompts at once (about 1.9M tokens live), all needles correct, 89.4 tok/s total with 2.5 GiB free on the 3090. With all K/V on the cards, four slots gave 111.4 tok/s total and 3.2 GiB free. The cost is the wait: the engine prefills one session at a time, so the eighth session got its first token after about 20 minutes, and each session decodes at 9-35 tok/s while it shares the cards. Separately, Unsloth's Dynamic V3.1 re-upload of Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_M runs 32.3 tok/s against 32.1 for the old file on one 3090, with the same retrievals and quality check; whether its claimed agentic gain is real waits on the paired agent runs.

metrics.label: Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 ~240k sessions held at once, both cards
Total decode, four ~240k prompts at once, all K/V on the cards

findings.quality: Every needle correct (8 of 8 and 4 of 4); both Qwen3.8-27B files 3 of 3 on the quality check.
findings.caveat: One run each. The 104.3 tok/s baseline is two ~240k prompts on the 3090 alone. Per-session first tokens at 240k range from about 2 to 20 minutes because prefill is serialised.

findings.title: webAI's TwIL-8B is fast and right once it may think long; Nex-N2.6 is correct but too slow to prefill; the RustingStrata engine works at about a third of Strata's speed
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates. TwIL-8B, webAI's new 8B reasoning model, runs on one 3090 at its native 128k: the balanced Q4_K_M file decodes 96.4 tok/s with first tokens under 0.1 s and both retrievals correct, and scores 3 of 3 on the quality check once the token cap is 16k (it used up to 5k tokens of thinking on a short Python task; at our usual caps every answer was cut off mid-thought). The verbose Q8_0 file decodes 72.6 tok/s, overthinks past 16k tokens on the same task and scores 1 of 3. Nex-N2.6, an agent post-train of GLM-5.3-Flash, at Q2_K across both cards with experts in RAM decodes 10.6 tok/s and answers correctly, but prefills at about 50 tok/s, so a 30k prompt waits about 10 minutes. RustingStrata 1.2.1, a pure-Rust engine, serves Flash-Next UD-Q2_K_XL on the 3090 at 34.7 tok/s (36.7 with its draft head) against 120.7 for Strata 0.2.13 on the same file, with both retrievals correct. Arete-27B Q6_K with three 256k slots does not fit on our two cards.

metrics.label: TwIL-8B balanced quality check, out of 3, usual caps to a 16k token cap
Flash-Next UD-Q2_K_XL decode on the 3090, Strata 0.2.13 to RustingStrata 1.2.1 (draft on)

findings.quality: TwIL-8B balanced 3 of 3 and verbose 1 of 3 with a 16k cap; Nex-N2.6 3 of 3; every retrieval correct except the verbose TwIL file at 120k, which found both markers but added their names.
findings.caveat: One run each. TwIL-8B is under a non-commercial licence. RustingStrata rates are measured at the client because the engine reports no server timings.

findings.title: Four ~250k agent sessions at once on both cards: Tiel-Coder and its abliterated twin fit and recall, but decode about 11 tok/s per session
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates, with the 3090 capped at 250 W and the V100 at 200 W. We are looking for an agent backend that serves four sessions of about 250k tokens at once across the 3090 and V100 at 40 tok/s or more per session. Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B UD-Q6_K_XL with four 256k slots fits (4.1 GiB free on the 3090, 2.9 GiB on the V100), decodes 107 tok/s on short prompts and recalls both markers at 250k, but with four ~240k prompts at once it decodes 43 tok/s in total, about 11 per session. The abliterated Cyber-Tiel-Coder gives the same numbers. At that depth attention dominates: four sessions give about the same total as one session at 250k (39.5 tok/s). The same load gives about 19 tok/s per session with four ~120k prompts and about 28 with four ~60k. Prefill runs one session at a time, so the fourth 240k session waits about 23 minutes for its first token. Arete-27B Q8_0 with two 256k slots fits but decodes 25 tok/s alone and 12.6 in total with two long sessions.

Tiel-Coder decode, one session at 250k to four sessions at ~240k (total)

findings.quality: Every marker correct: the 250k retrievals and all four streams in every run.
findings.caveat: One run each, greedy, thinking off, power-capped until a bigger power supply is in. Per-session rates are totals while all streams decode, divided by four.

findings.title: Four ~250k agent sessions at once: 16-bit K/V nearly doubles decode, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning reaches about 35 tok/s per session
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates, with the 3090 capped at 250 W and the V100 at 200 W, four sessions on both cards, thinking off. The 8-bit K/V cache was the bottleneck at depth: Tiel-Coder with four ~120k prompts goes from about 19 tok/s per session with 8-bit K/V to about 34 with 16-bit (F16), and F16 also needs less memory than 8-bit for the same slots on this engine. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Q8_0 with F16 K/V gives about 35 tok/s per session with four ~240k prompts and about 45 with four ~120k, every answer correct, with 7 GiB free on the 3090 and 6.5 GiB on the V100. It also reads long prompts more than twice as fast as Tiel-Coder (about 1,680 against 710 tok/s), so the fourth 240k session gets its first token after about 10 minutes instead of 24. Tiel-Coder UD-Q4_K_XL with F16 K/V reaches about 25 per session at ~240k. ThinkingCap-27B Heretic does not fit four 256k slots. None reaches 40 tok/s per session at ~240k; Nemotron is the pick for the next step, four OpenCode agents at once.

Four ~240k sessions, per-session decode, Tiel-Coder Q6 8-bit K/V to Nemotron Lightning F16 K/V

findings.quality: Every marker correct in all four streams of every run, and Nemotron's 250k retrieval correct.
findings.caveat: One run each, greedy, thinking off, power-capped until a bigger power supply is in. Per-session rates are totals while all streams decode, divided by four. Agent quality with four sessions at once is not measured yet.

findings.title: Four OpenCode agents at once on one Nemotron 3.5 Lightning load: the serving holds, the code mostly does not
findings.summary: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Q8_0 with 16-bit K/V and four 256k slots across both cards (power-capped) served four OpenCode agents at once for two hours: tests 1, 2, 7 and test 1 again, thinking off, temperature 0.6. Every session ran without a harness error. Agent-run rates while the others ran: 35.5, 38.1 and 41.8 tok/s per session, 61.1 for the labyrinth once it ran alone; server first token median 0.25 s over 890 requests; 7.1 GiB free on the 3090 and 6.6 GiB on the V100 throughout. One of four results is clean: the first test 1 passes every live check with 26 of its own tests passing in 13.5 minutes. The second test 1 never handled the login, test 2 builds and passes its own 7 tests but its server answers only after its input closes, and the labyrinth scored 0 on the automatic checks. In the same round Flint Preview 40B-A2.5B fit four 256k slots but lost recall at 250k (a repetition loop) and ran about 7 tok/s per session at ~240k, so Nemotron stays the pick of five candidates.

findings.quality: 1 of 4 agent results clean (test 1); test 7 graded on the automatic checks only, walk and notes not judged yet.
findings.caveat: One run, one load, power-capped until a bigger power supply is in. Nemotron's single-session agent results on these tests are not measured, so this does not show whether running four at once costs quality.

findings.title: Tiel-Coder with thinking off spends 28.6 hours on the labyrinth and hands in nothing
findings.summary: Agent-run rates, OpenCode. Tiel-Coder-35B Q6 across the 3090 and V100 with thinking off ran test 7 for 28.6 hours without writing the generator, the maze or its notes, so it scored 0 of 10. The conversation filled to about 107k tokens about 80 times; each time OpenCode compacted it to about 7k and the model restarted its maze design from scratch, leaving about 700 lines of unfinished generator, 66 throwaway probe scripts and two design notes. It ran at 82.0 tok/s (first token median 0.44 s) over 9,584 requests and 5.25 million output tokens. We stopped it by hand and are rerunning the same case with OpenCode's dynamic context pruning plugin to see whether pruning breaks the loop.

metrics.label: Labyrinth score, GSQ IQ3_XXS to Tiel-Coder thinking off
Labyrinth wall time, GSQ IQ3_XXS to Tiel-Coder thinking off

findings.quality: Tiel-Coder thinking off, test 7: A 0, B 0, C 0 (no maze, no generator), D 0 and E 0 (nothing to walk, no notes).
findings.caveat: One run. OpenCode, not T3 Code. Stopped by hand at 28.6 hours; the brief allows three hours, but our agent runs have no time cap.

findings.title: Context pruning ends Tiel-Coder's compaction loop, but the labyrinth still scores 0
findings.summary: Agent-run rates, OpenCode. We reran Tiel-Coder-35B Q6 (3090 + V100, thinking off) on test 7 with OpenCode's dynamic context pruning plugin. The loop that sank the first run is gone: the model pruned its own history 13 times, OpenCode never compacted, and the prompt peaked near 107k tokens. It ran at 84.7 tok/s (first token median 0.51 s) over 1,062 requests. After 2.5 hours it wrote a file-write tool call as plain text, OpenCode read that as the final reply, and the run ended with an unfinished generator and no maze, so it scored 0 of 10 again.

findings.title: Two OpenCode agents share one 3090: test 2 passes beside a second session; switching between parked 155k sessions takes 1.25 s
findings.summary: Agent serving profile (UD-Q2_K_XL, MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W): two 256k slots, 20,480 K/V cells per layer in VRAM, the rest in pinned host RAM, and a 28 GiB session cache in host RAM. Short-benchmark rates: with 4 and then 6 sessions of about 155k tokens served in rotation, a switch back to a parked session gives its first token in 1.25 s median instead of 60 s cold, all 30 recalls right, about 3 GiB of host RAM per parked session. Four 256k slots also fit and keep the total: four ~120k prompts at once decode 95.8 tok/s together (about 20-27 each). Agent run: OpenCode ran test 1 and test 2 at the same time on one load; test 2 passed in full (8 tools, 113 of its own tests) at 39.2 tok/s per session, about 77 summed, first token median 1.36 s with prompts up to 217k tokens, and the engine parked and restored sessions from host RAM inside the run. The test 1 session was cut by our own thermal check, not graded.

findings.quality: Test 2 full pass (builds, initialize, 8 tools, real tool call, 113/0 own tests); all 30 switch recalls and all 6 concurrent streams correct.

findings.title: UD-Q3_K_XL builds the best Flash-Next labyrinth (10 of 10); the agent serving profile passes test 1 beside a second agent
findings.summary: Test 7, the three-floor labyrinth generator, on UD-Q3_K_XL with the daily-driver engine setup (MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W, Qwen thinking sampling) scores 10 of 10 in 53 minutes at 108.2 tok/s agent-run decode with a 0.58 s median first token. Its maze has no entrance tunnel, evenly spread stairs and real side passages, where UD-Q2_K_XL's (9 of 10, 38 minutes, 119.5 tok/s) was a comb of one-cell dead ends. On the agent serving profile (two 256k slots, sessions parked in host RAM), OpenCode ran test 1 and test 7 at the same time: test 1 passed every live check with 14 subcommands and 205 of its own tests in 40 minutes at 74.1 tok/s, first token median 0.49 s with prompts up to 196k tokens. A session left idle for 30 minutes came back from host RAM with its first token in 1.85 s. The test 7 session scored 0: its second request thought for the full 24,000-token reasoning budget and the forced answer had no tool call, so OpenCode ended the session with no files.

findings.quality: Test 7 A 2, B 2, C 2, D 2, E 2 (every claim in its notes reproduced); agent-profile test 1 passes 5 of 5 live checks, 205/0 own tests; agent-profile test 7 A-E 0 (no files).

findings.title: The V100 adds 14% to four parallel agent streams; UD-Q2_0 is as fast as UD-Q2_K_XL; Arete-27B passes test 1 on the V100
findings.summary: Short-benchmark rates. On the agent serving profile with four 256k slots, adding the V100 as a peer tier raises total decode with four ~120k prompts at once from 95.8 to 109.6 tok/s, and with two from 91.4 to 101.1; with two slots the same peer tier was inside the noise. All six streams were right and both cards fit (3.1 GiB free on the 3090, 2.2 GiB on the V100). The smaller UD-Q2_0 quant (65.7 GiB against 74.1 GiB) on the daily-driver setup at 300 W decodes 122.4 tok/s against 120.7 for UD-Q2_K_XL, with both long retrievals right and first tokens of 10.6 and 42.7 s at 30k and 120k; its agent tests decide between them. Agent run: Arete-27B Q6_K on the V100 alone passed test 1 (every live check, 11 subcommands, 59 of its own tests) in 60 minutes at 18.4 tok/s, first token median 0.61 s.

findings.quality: Peer tier: 6 of 6 streams recall both markers; UD-Q2_0: 30k and 120k retrievals right; Arete-27B test 1: 5 of 5 live checks, 59/0 own tests.
findings.caveat: One sample each. Three of the four 120k streams hit the 12,000-token reply limit. The Arete run is OpenCode, not T3 Code; its first attempt the same night never started (a sandbox network bug on our side) and is not a result.

findings.title: UD-Q2_0 matches the daily driver's quality and runs about 13% faster in agent runs
findings.summary: Agent-run rates, Qwen thinking sampling, one 3090 at 300 W, OpenCode. The smaller UD-Q2_0 quant (65.7 GiB) passed agent test 1 with every live check, 25 subcommands and 471 of its own tests passing (64 minutes, 136.6 tok/s decode, first token median 0.33 s), test 2T with 9 tools and 85 tests passing while using only the real endpoints (33 minutes, 137.0 tok/s, median 0.39 s), and scored 9 of 10 on the labyrinth (44 minutes, 135.3 tok/s, median 0.25 s). UD-Q2_K_XL on the same setup decoded 119-123 tok/s in its agent runs and also scored 9 on the labyrinth; UD-Q3_K_XL scored 10 at about 108 tok/s. Both 2-bit quants fit with 2.2 GiB free.

findings.quality: Test 1: 5 of 5 live checks, 471/0 own tests. Test 2T: builds, 9 tools, tool call works, 85/0 tests, trust verdict tested. Test 7: A 2, B 2, C 2, D 1, E 2.
findings.caveat: One run each. The short benchmark showed only a 1-2% speed gap, so the agent-run gain may partly be run-to-run variation. Test 2 is still running. OpenCode, not T3 Code.

findings.title: UD-Q2_0 passes all four agent tests; a 3-bit GSQ quant passes test 1 but is 14% slower
findings.summary: Agent-run rates, Qwen thinking sampling, one 3090 at 300 W, OpenCode. findings.title: Flash-Next on one 3090: 162 tok/s on code and 203 on JSON with a DFlash2 draft model
findings.summary: The 150 tok/s goal is met for code and JSON output. On Strata 0.2.13 with the 128.6 setup, a DFlash2 draft model reaches 156.8 tok/s on code and 198.25 on JSON on UD-IQ3_XXS, and 162.25 / 203.1 on UD-Q2_K_XL, against 147.0 / 178.85 for the MTP head. Prose stays at about 120-128 tok/s. Every setup passed a three-task quality check (a Python task run in a sandbox, a JSON extraction, a word problem). Letting Strata pick the drafter itself is slower than either fixed choice (101 tok/s on prose). A 256k slot fits on the 3090 alone with a 4,096 MiB VRAM reserve: a 248k-token retrieval was correct with the first token in 94.7 s (2,628 tok/s prefill) and 2.2 GiB free. Four 128k slots also fit, but Strata prefills prompts one at a time and drafts almost nothing once two streams decode together, so four streams sum to only 123-126 tok/s; llama.cpp on a model that fits in VRAM (Tiel-Coder 35B) goes from 97 to 165 tok/s.

findings.title: Flash-Next code output at 168 tok/s with a fit check, and it holds when sampled like an agent
findings.summary: On UD-Q2_K_XL with a DFlash2 draft model and a draft window of 8, Strata 0.2.13 reaches 167.55 tok/s on code, 206 on JSON and 154.8 on mixed prose and code, and still keeps 2.2 GiB free after a 120k-token prompt (first token 42.2 s, 2,847 tok/s prefill). A 256k slot with the DFlash2 draft model also fits and stays above 150 on code and JSON (152.85-157.95 and 191-197 tok/s; first token at 248k in about 93 s). Sampling like an agent instead of greedy decoding leaves the MTP head unchanged and costs DFlash2 about 10% on code (150.5 tok/s). A lower draft confidence, coupled draft sampling and a memory clock lock changed nothing; four slots with DFlash2 sum to 127 tok/s but miss our fit rule. llamAmpere with four slots is far slower (46-83 tok/s total, 30k prompts prefill at 234 tok/s). Keeping the K/V cache in host RAM on llama.cpp cuts decode about five times.

findings.title: Four Flash-Next slots fit on one 3090, and two 100k slots fit too

Two slots with ~100k prompts each also fit (3.2 GiB free) and sum to 103.1 tok/s; the second prompt waits for the first, so its first token takes 88.5 s against 35.4 s alone. findings.title: A host-RAM session cache makes switching between long sessions 37 times faster; two 256k agent slots fit on one 3090
findings.summary: Daily driver (UD-Q2_K_XL, MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W), short-benchmark rates. With a 12 GiB session cache in host RAM, returning to a 93k-token session that another one displaced gives its first token in 0.93 s median instead of 34.8 s, because 99.9% of the prompt is reused; it costs 2-2.8 GiB of host RAM per parked session and no VRAM. Batch slots alone do not keep sessions (35.9 s). For agent serving, two 256k slots with two ~240k prompts at once fit on every setup tried with at least 2.1 GiB free per card. Keeping the whole K/V in 3090 VRAM starves the expert cache (51.5 tok/s total); keeping 20,480 cells per layer in VRAM and the rest in pinned host RAM gives 90.2 tok/s total with the fastest second prompt (first token 235 s). Adding the V100, as a peer tier or a layer split, gives 94-101 tok/s, one sample each, so all of these are one band.

findings.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs across a 3090 and a V100
findings.summary: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017 UD-IQ1_S now serves from two different cards, an RTX 3090 24 GB and a Tesla V100 32 GB, with the routed experts in RAM and a GPU expert cache. Short-benchmark decode rose from 9.7 tok/s on the starting config (20 GiB cache, F16 KV, flash attention off) to 16.5 tok/s with a 34 GiB cache, flash attention and Q8 KV at 96k context. Raising ubatch from 512 to 2048 cut the 30k-token first-token time from 14.3 to 6.1 minutes (35 to 83 tok/s prefill). A 90,230-token retrieval at 96k context was correct in every config tried; its first token came after 48.5 minutes at ubatch 512 and 21.7 minutes with a 30 GiB cache and ubatch 2048 (69 tok/s prefill). The two levers compete for the 3090: a 34 GiB cache with ubatch 1024 keeps the best decode (16.4 tok/s) but leaves 1.6 GiB free, just inside our 1.5 GiB rule; a 30 GiB cache with ubatch 2048 gives the fastest long prompts at 14.5 tok/s decode; moving layers to the V100 (split 3:2) frees the 3090 but costs about 1.4 tok/s. A 40 GiB cache does not fit: the V100 runs out of memory at load.

findings.title: Flash-Next on one 3090: 129 tok/s, and 127 tok/s right after a 120k prompt
findings.summary: Toward a goal of 150 tok/s decode and 1,000+ tok/s prefill on a larger Unsloth v3.1 quant of Flash-Next, Strata 0.2.12 on one RTX 3090 reached 128.6 tok/s short-benchmark decode on UD-IQ3_XXS (from 98.8): power 250 to 350 W gave +13%, an English and code draft vocabulary +2%, and a per-token (stream) draft-head norm with a draft min-p of 0.6 most of the rest, by raising draft acceptance from about 55% to 60-68%. Prefill is met: with a K/V cache that grows with the context, a 120,007-token retrieval was correct with the first token in 40.2 s (2,987 tok/s). Strata's adaptive fetch (margin 0, PCIe share 0.55) holds 124-127 tok/s right after that long prompt on the 3090 alone. With the V100 as a peer tier that computes its cached experts, decode stays at 119 tok/s after a 30k prompt and 128 after 120k, and four 128k slots keep 109 tok/s per stream. Twenty more single-change runs found nothing faster: CPU pool and thread placement, prompt chunk size, a high-priority graph stream and a DFlash2 draft model (7.5% slower on our prose prompts) all tied or lost, and two replicates (127.6, 127.7) confirm the 128.6 base. The same setup gives 123.0 tok/s on UD-Q2_K_XL and 112.0 on UD-Q3_K_XL. On the peer tier the quant barely matters: Q2_K_XL ties IQ3_XXS at 107 tok/s. Locking Strata's PLE table in RAM is neutral (122.5 on the 3090 alone, 104-110 on the peer-tier setups, all within noise), Strata 0.2.13 ties 0.2.12 (126.1 tok/s on the 3090 alone, 109.4 on the peer tier), and llamAmpere 0.6.3.8 ties 0.6.3.2 (85.1 tok/s).

findings.title: DeepSeek at 256k, and two sessions at once
findings.summary: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, UD-IQ1_S, 8-bit KV. Six GPU layers instead of seven: a strict 128-token decode on a 251,590-token prompt rose from 2.71 to 3.09 tok/s and the text matched. Nonce isolation was measured at about 8.8k tokens per session: each session answered only its own nonce. The 96k figure is decode depth only: 3.70 tok/s alone, 2.74 each when both ran (5.58 combined). Restoring the saved cache returned the same reply, including a vision answer.

findings.quality: The pagoda half and the workflow half, each 0 to 10, were not scored.
findings.caveat: One run. The project directory was deleted afterward and the page was rebuilt from the edit log. This is not a score on the frozen rubric.

findings.title: DeepSeek Maya-XS passes the graded agent tests
findings.summary: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Maya-XS on Maya 1.1.28 passed every graded agent run. Test 1 was 5 of 5 checks, with 37 tests then 50. Test 2 exposed 8 tools then 7, and passed 45 tests then 19. The planted-docs run exposed 8 tools, passed 31 tests, and hedged: it tried the planted endpoints, then shipped the real ones first. Test 3 was 14 of 14 on both flavors in both rounds, with rubrics 11, 12, 12 and 11, and the judgement was right each time. All three test-4 tickets passed, with 4, 13 and 11 hidden checks and no failed own tests.
findings.settings: Maya 1.1.28, Maya-XS IQ1_S, max context 131072, vision off; DSpark state not recorded per case
findings.quality: No graded agent run failed. The planted-docs code kept the real endpoints first. Test 3 judgements were right in both rounds.
findings.caveat: Two runs for tests 1, 2 and 3. Both rounds of test 4 are scored. Round 2 of the planted-docs test is scored. Round-2 test 2 was already scored. Minutes exclude model-load time. The tok/s figure includes tool time. Context is the served max of 131072; these case dirs have no spec snapshot, and the KV type was not recorded.

findings.title: DeepSeek one-shots: round 1 packaging scored 0, the final block did not
findings.summary: Round 1 orrery is 7 of 10 on the final code block (1, 2, 2, 1, 1): four inner planets at the real period ratios, moving arms, and gears that do not mesh. The harness join of that whole reply does not parse, so the packaged file scores 0. Round 1 pagoda is 10 of 10 on the final page and 0 on the harness join, which stops on a syntax error. Round 2 has no reply leak. The orrery file as delivered is 9 of 10 (2, 2, 2, 1, 2): six planets, Uranus and Neptune absent, gears that do not follow the gear law. The pagoda file as delivered is 10 of 10.

metrics.label: Orrery, final block then delivered file
Pagoda, final block then delivered file

findings.quality: Round 2 pages run as delivered. Round 1 scores are of the final block, not of the harness file.
findings.caveat: One run each. Both rounds have gallery frames and live pieces; round 1 shows the graded final block, not the broken harness extract. Decode on the one-shots was 26.1 and 27.9 tok/s, then 26.0 and 26.2.

findings.title: DeepSeek Maya-XS bench decode is ahead of the agent runs
findings.summary: A short bench of the same entry, temperature 0 and 400 tokens, measured 31.0 tok/s on code, 18.9 on prose and 32.2 on structured output. Agent test 1, which includes tool time, was 23.2 tok/s then 22.6.
findings.quality: Not an agent grade. The agent runs above are the quality evidence.
findings.caveat: One bench, taken just before round 1. It is not a paired before-and-after.

findings.title: GPU unlock raises long-prompt prefill by 43%
findings.summary: On our 3090 box, vLLM Qwen3.8-27B was measured with GPU unlock off, then on, then on again. A 140826-token prompt prefilled at 736 tok/s off. Unlock rounds were 1053 and 1056 tok/s on seed 41, and 1053 and 1055 tok/s on seed 42. The probe summary calls that a 43.3% and 43.2% gain. Short code decode moved from 126.4 to 127.9 and 127.5 tok/s. The same check on llama.cpp 0.7 with Tiel left short code decode at 149.1, 148.6 and 148.8 tok/s.
findings.quality: The needle check passed in every unlock phase, on and off.
findings.caveat: One off-round and two on-rounds, one card. Short decode barely moved. Tiel long-prompt prefill rose less (2201 to 2397 tok/s on seed 41, 1549 to 1746 on seed 42) and its deep decode stayed 97.7 tok/s on seed 41. The llama.cpp version is from the same day's entry spec, not from a spec file inside the probe directory.

findings.title: Flash-Next Heretic 2 passes the coding tests and fails both one-shots
findings.summary: Test 1 scored 5 of 5 checks, 36 tests and 0 failures at 18.2 tok/s. Test 2 built, initialized, exposed 7 tools, called a tool, and passed 34 tests with 0 failures. Three test-4 tickets passed, with 4, 13 and 11 hidden checks. The orrery one-shot scored 0 of 10 because the SVG did not parse. The pagoda one-shot scored 0 of 10 because every sealed frame was only the clear color.
findings.quality: Code tests passed. One-shots did not render a usable scene.
findings.caveat: One run each. The trust-variant test 2 exposed 4 tools and passed 28 tests; that is a different case, not a failure of the 7-tool run.

findings.title: Ornith 122B and Defiance pass tests 1 and 2
findings.summary: Ornith UD-Q4_K_XL scored 5 of 5 CLI checks and 48 tests at 13.4 tok/s, then a 7-tool server with 43 tests and 0 failures at 12.9 tok/s. Defiance IQ4_XS at 196608 context scored 5 of 5 checks and 82 tests at 32.5 tok/s, then 7 tools, 46 tests and 0 failures at 22.6 tok/s.
findings.quality: Both protocol suites passed. No new one-shot grade for either model in this window.
findings.caveat: One run each. Ornith has no spec snapshot, so context and KV are unknown. Defiance one-shots finished later and are not graded.

findings.title: Orca uncensored passes test 4; its trust tests did not compile
findings.summary: Test 1 scored 5 of 5 checks and 41 tests. The plain test 2 built, initialized, exposed 9 tools and passed 42 tests. Three test-4 tickets passed (4, 13 and 11 hidden checks). The trust run also built, initialized and called tools (9 tools), but cargo test exited 101 while compiling. The parsed 0 and 0 counts are not a suite pass.
findings.quality: Coding tickets passed. Trust-run test quality is incomplete, not a pass.
findings.caveat: The plain test-2 grade is in the prerequisite regrade file, not the main grade table. Test 3 for this model is not in the canonical grade table.

findings.title: Heretic 2 judges a known-good server right and its own server wrong
findings.summary: On the known-good server, MCP and REST were both 14 of 14 and the judgement was right (rubric 12). On its own server, REST was 14 of 14 and MCP 13 of 14. The fixed server builds, initializes, exposes 7 tools and passes 34 tests, but the missing fact is temperature and the final judgement is wrong (rubric 9).
findings.quality: Fact match was high. The own-server trust decision was wrong.
findings.caveat: One run of each flavor. Minutes use the run duration without model-load time.

findings.title: An expert cache makes Flash-Next 1.5x faster on one 3090
findings.summary: Qwen3.8 Flash-Next (125B, 6B active) does not fit in 24 GB, so llama.cpp keeps experts in system RAM. Keeping all of them there (-cmoe) and giving the GPU a cache of hot experts (--moe-cache-mib), with q8 KV to make room, beat the old split of 40 layers on CPU on every GGUF tried, at 262k context.
findings.quality: Against the old f16 KV config: mean KL 0.0011 and 98 % top-1 agreement over 100k tokens of real code; two loads of the same config differ by KL 0.0002. Needles found at 100k, 190k and 250k.
findings.caveat: Lazy tensor reads (llama.cpp's default) make the first pass over unseen text slow when the page cache is cold; -lzm off fixes it but costs about 28 GB of extra RAM. Raw decode with short outputs is higher (25-37 tok/s on orca). The tqLLM control run measured the same GGUF at about 40 tok/s on short outputs; that measure is higher than the streamed one.

findings.title: Strata 0.2.2 is 17% faster than 0.2.0
findings.summary: Same-day control on the Gyro-S build with an MTP draft: code decode rose from 121.6 to 144.1 tok/s, prose from 106.4 to 123.4.
findings.quality: Tool call and needle probes passed on both builds.
findings.caveat: One load per engine; no agent run on 0.2.2 yet.

findings.title: Flint: a 40B coding MoE fits the card
findings.summary: Flint (39.8B total, about 2.5B active, Apache-2.0) at Q3_K_XL runs entirely on the GPU at 262k context with q8 KV.

metrics.label: Decode, Q4_K_XL, 15 expert layers in RAM

findings.quality: Not graded: no test has been run, and its one-shots are ungraded.
findings.caveat: Needs llama.cpp b11803 or newer; f16 KV does not fit. Q4_K_XL slows from 81 to 64 tok/s as more experts move to RAM.

findings.title: tqLLM serves Flash-Next fast but not for agents
findings.summary: tqLLM 1.2.3 decodes Flash-Next about 2.5x faster than llama.cpp on the same GGUF, but one prefill out-of-memory leaves every later request failing until a restart.
findings.quality: Tool calls and a 30k needle passed at 32k; at 262k with 8k prefill chunks it found a needle in 248k tokens. At 131072 context it failed on a 289-token prompt, and every later request failed until a restart.
findings.caveat: Short replies with thinking off; any prompt of 256+ tokens can trigger the failure. First load took 23 minutes cold.

findings.title: Stock Flash-Next at 200k with vision, 24-25 tok/s
findings.summary: The stock Flash-Next EXL3 3-bit build on SGLang with an fp8 KV cache serves 204,800 tokens of context and images at 24-25 tok/s, two sessions at once.
findings.quality: Tools, vision and 11 of 11 multi-session checks pass; needle found at 100k, 150k and 190k; a repeated 190k prompt answers in 0.5 s.

findings.title: Stock SGLang now serves Flash-Next to 11 of 11 sessions
findings.summary: Three stock SGLang builds of Flash-Next, 204,800 context and two slots, all passed the multi-session probe and needles at 100k, 150k and 190k.
findings.quality: Needles found at 100k, 150k and 190k; prefill about 2,600 tok/s.
findings.caveat: The phased build was dropped; no agent test was run on these builds in this round.

findings.title: Ornith-1.5-122B reaches 16 tok/s on one card
findings.summary: A 122B Qwen3.5 mixture (8 of 256 experts per token) at UD-Q4_K_XL with 262k context and q8 KV, sweeping how many expert layers stay on the CPU.
findings.quality: Deep-prompt decode 15.8 tok/s at 40 layers; larger batches lift prefill from 118 to 392 tok/s.
findings.caveat: Not graded: one-shots ran at about 15 tok/s but were not scored, and no test has been run.

findings.title: Gyro-S + MTP: a competent 24-minute test-2 run
findings.summary: Flash-Next in Gyro-S (TQ1_0) on Strata 0.2.0-beta with an MTP draft decodes 119 tok/s on code, passes test 2 in full and scores 9 of 10 on the agent pagoda.
findings.quality: Test 2: 6 tools, 108 tests, none failing; tool call, needles at 16k and 64k and the test-1 smoke all passed.
findings.caveat: One run. The comparison arm is the IQ3_S quant on the same engine; Strata 0.2.0 was in beta.

findings.title: Tools and a browser rescue blank pagodas
findings.summary: Six models whose one-shot pagoda was blank scored 7 to 10 once they ran as agents with a sealed browser.
findings.quality: Same rubric and offline renders for both; the six are Coder 390, ThinkingCap, Orcarouter, Abliterated s1.5, Cyber and Cyber Q5.
findings.caveat: One agent run per model; orrery results are mixed (0 to 10) and some test-8 runs are not graded yet.

findings.title: Maya 1.1.11 fixes split digits and speeds up
findings.summary: On the same GLM-5.3-Flash pack, Maya 1.1.11 copied all 12 digit strings exactly and found both needles; 1.0.4 split one string and found one needle.
findings.quality: Maya-S and Maya-M on 1.1.13 also scored 12 of 12 with both needles.
findings.caveat: Two rounds per version.

findings.title: exllamav3 1.6.2 matches 1.6.1
findings.summary: The DFlash2 build of Qwen3.8-27B on exllamav3 1.6.2 decodes as fast as on 1.6.1 and finds the needle at 128k, 112k and 94k.
findings.quality: Needle 48213-KESTREL found at all three windows.
findings.caveat: Two rounds each; the difference is within noise.

findings.title: Saluki: a 2-bit Qwen3.8-27B that still calls tools
findings.summary: A 2-bit tune of Qwen3.8-27B (7.9 GB) passed test 1 with 72 tests and part-passed test 2, with 17 tools.
findings.quality: Graded by the standard test 1 and test 2 graders.
findings.caveat: Test 2 was partial (166 minutes at 22.0 tok/s); one run each.

findings.title: LFM2.5-24B is fast but passes no test 2
findings.summary: Five quants of LFM2.5-24B decoded at 125 to 176 tok/s on test 1 and passed it in three of five; none passed test 2.
findings.quality: Graded by the standard graders; test-2 servers had 0 to 3 tools.
findings.caveat: Test-1 runs were often two minutes long, so the test counts are small.

findings.title: Strata 0.1.44.1 doubles decode
findings.summary: Flash-Next on Strata, two rounds each: 0.1.44.1 loaded in a mean 60 s against 214 s, and decoded 44.9 tok/s against 18.3.
findings.quality: Same prompts and engine settings in all rounds.
findings.caveat: The first 0.1.42 round was cold; its warm round decoded 23.5 tok/s, so the true gain is nearer 1.9 times. Load time: 60 s against 214 s on the round mean, but the warm 0.1.42 round loaded in 41.5 s.

findings.title: Thinking models fail the one-shot pagoda
findings.summary: Qwen3.8-27B on vLLM with thinking on ran out of length in seven tries; with thinking off the three pages were blank.
findings.quality: Identical blank pages in the thinking-off tries.
findings.caveat: Other stacks also scored 0 on some tries: Tiel Coder one of five, Gemma-4-26B-A4B one of five, exllamav3 MTP five of six.

findings.title: Speed at 141k context
findings.summary: Four stacks timed on code with a 141k-token history: Gemma-4-26B-A4B with an MTP draft stays fastest, though it loses the most (54 %).
findings.quality: Needle found at 141k by all four.
findings.caveat: Prefill at that depth: 2,094, 2,046, 739 and about 650 tok/s.

findings.title: Engine shoot-out on Qwen3.8-27B
findings.summary: Drafting lifts decode from 42 tok/s to 95 to 170 tok/s on code; TensorFold with DFlash2 is fastest but holds the smallest window.
findings.quality: At temperature 0 drafting changed 7 of 15 exllamav3 DFlash2 replies, 10 of 15 with MTP, 4 of 15 on llama.cpp and none on TensorFold.
findings.caveat: The window with an 8-bit cache is 98k (exllamav3 DFlash2), 131k (MTP) and 43 to 73k (TensorFold). Baselines are each engine without drafting.

findings.title: Test 4: Tiel Coder fixes 9 of 9 tickets
findings.summary: Three tickets in a known-good Rust crate, three runs each: every run passed all hidden checks with no regressions and no false 'done'.
findings.quality: Hidden black-box checks (4, 11 and 13 per ticket) plus the crate's 155 tests; runs finished with 156 to 168 passing tests.
findings.caveat: One model only; the slowest run took 42 minutes.

findings.title: Old PCIe share doubles Flash-Next on Strata 0.1.42
findings.summary: Setting the old PCIe share on Strata 0.1.42 raised long-answer decode from 48 to 95 tok/s and big-prompt reads from 1,177 to 1,983 tok/s.
findings.quality: Test 1 passed in 51 minutes instead of 94; test 2 passed with 77 tests in 61 minutes instead of 98 (72 tests).
findings.caveat: Two probe rounds per variant; one agent run each.

findings.title: Grader audit changes four test-1 verdicts
findings.summary: All 125 archived test-1 and test-2 runs were regraded after fixing the graders; four test-1 verdicts changed.
findings.quality: Changes: Bonsai ada fail to pass, a Flash-Next row and a Qwen3.8 row partial to pass, Devstral Small 2 pass to partial.
findings.caveat: Twelve other rows had test counts corrected; six rows lost a no-crash tick.

findings.title: Maya patches take GLM-5.3-Flash to 19 tok/s
findings.summary: Two engine patches lifted decode from 3.95 to 18.7 tok/s; the model then passed test 1 (44 tests) and test 2 (7 tools, 66 tests, 322 minutes).
findings.quality: Standard graders; both tests passed.
findings.caveat: Decode figures come from the run log, not a result file. A 1-bit variant failed both tests.

overall.verdict: Built the best test-2 server of every run.
overall.tradeoff: Slower than the 27B stacks. The earlier build crashed under several sessions; the current stock builds served 11 of 11 sessions at about 25 tok/s on 2026-10-21, though no agent test has been rerun on them.

overall.verdict: Full passes on both tests; the default agent model.
overall.tradeoff: The same weights on llama.cpp scored the same and ran 2-4x slower.

uncensored.verdict: Orcarouter fine-tune of Flash-Next; full test-2 pass with long-horizon settings, the most tools and tests and the fewest compiler errors of the big uncensored runs.
uncensored.tradeoff: Slow: 7.6 tok/s, 191 min. Flash-Next Heretic2 is twice as fast for a thinner result (7 tools, 33 tests in 120 min).

uncensored.verdict: Two test-2 full passes and 5/5 on test 1; run it with the thinking budget.
uncensored.tradeoff: OrcaSAQ-2-Cyber is faster (about 80 tok/s) but one of its two test-2 runs shipped a broken HTTP client.

families.note: vLLM with MTP drafts at 150k context is both: llama.cpp on the same weights scored the same and ran 2-4x slower. Uncensored: the AWQ uncensored checkpoint is the steadier, OrcaSAQ the faster (DFlash2) but variable.
SGLang built the best server; Strata runs the GSQ-RCO quants at 21-24 tok/s over a run with full passes. Only llama.cpp runs the uncensored tunes (0.6 is 2.5-4x faster than 0.4).
IQ4_XS is the fastest model that writes working test-1 code (101 tok/s) but its test-2 server called an invented endpoint; the Q6 security tune passed test 2.
Good on test 1, both failed test 2 (no initialize / no tools). Superseded by Qwen3.8.
Fast (45-91 tok/s) but thin: 3 tools on test 2. Needs enable_thinking.
Test 1 thin, test 2 partial (no initialize); ~19 tok/s. Not competitive here.
GLM-4.7-Flash rejected numeric JSON-RPC ids, GLM-4.5-Air never answered initialize and ran at 3-6 tok/s. Dropped.
Nano 30B quit within minutes (2/5 twice); Super 120B passed test 1 with no tests at 8.5 tok/s. Not taken to test 2.
Devstral Small 2, Bonsai 2 (invented APIs), Nanbeige 3B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Jan Nano: inconsistent or failing on test 1. Excluded.

timeline.title: One prompt, Pi agent, API coverage
timeline.what: Write a Python CLI for the Home Assistant REST API. Pi agent, llama.cpp only, 17 cases. Scored by endpoints touched (of 9) and whether the code compiles.
timeline.why: A first look at which local models write working code at all.

timeline.title: Build an MCP server, then use one
timeline.what: OpenCode in a container against a recorded Home Assistant. Test 2: build a Rust MCP server from the spec on disk. Test 3A/3B: describe the house through your own server / someone else's.
timeline.why: Separate building a tool from using one; test 1 did not separate models.

timeline.title: Can uncensored Flash-Next still do the work?
timeline.what: Three uncensored Flash-Next routes (orcarouter fine-tune, Heretic2, abliterated s1.5) plus the stock model through the MCP test.
timeline.why: Red-team work on our own software needs models that do not refuse.

timeline.title: Offloaded models produced zero output
timeline.what: mmap + experts in RAM page-faulted the weights off NFS during the first request. Fix: -lm none (load eagerly). Also: 3 h case cap, longer client timeouts, guaranteed result records.
timeline.why: Several early 'failures' were the harness, not the model.

timeline.title: Test 1 graded by running the tool
timeline.what: Same CLI task, now graded by executing it in a sandbox: entry point + help, real reads, bad input, bad auth, no crash, plus the model's own tests. fill_vram tunes context and offload per model with real loads.
timeline.why: Counting endpoints in the source credited argparse help text and invented APIs.

timeline.title: Test 2 graded by driving the server
timeline.what: The Rust MCP server is built and spoken to as a real MCP client: initialize, tools/list, a real tools/call against the replay. Every failure verified by hand.
timeline.why: Test 2 separates models that test 1 cannot: invented endpoints, broken handshakes, networking bugs.

timeline.title: Context margin and thinking budget
timeline.what: OpenCode is told the context limit minus max(10%, 16k); a thinking budget of min(24k, reply cap − 6k) on every engine.
timeline.why: Runs died on context overflow, and on single thinks that ate the whole reply.

timeline.title: vLLM, SGLang, Strata
timeline.what: vLLM (HyperQwen) for the dense 27B, SGLang (EXL3) and Strata for Flash-Next, each behind llama-swap as a container.
timeline.why: Engine mattered as much as model: same weights, 2-5x speed.

timeline.title: A second llama.cpp, and long-horizon runs
timeline.what: Official llama.cpp v0.6.0 A/B against 0.4.1; 8 h long-horizon test 2 with Qwen's own long-run sampling; small-window vLLM profiles with OpenCode and Pi; Kolibri.
timeline.why: 0.6.0 is 2.5-4x faster on Flash-Next MoE; the uncensored Flash-Next finally finished test 2.

timeline.title: Long runs for the slower uncensored models
timeline.what: ThinkingCap-27B Heretic (new), and 8 h test 2 for Flash-Next Heretic2, Abliterated s1.5 and q38-27b-cyber.
timeline.why: Find the smartest uncensored model, not just the fastest.

timeline.title: Use an MCP server through a subagent, and fix it
timeline.what: The agent gets an MCP server's source and a subagent whose only tools are that server's. It must extract 14 facts through the subagent, check them against the REST API and fix the server if it is wrong. 3G: a known-good server; 3O: the model's own test-2 server. Transcripts scored on a 12-point rubric.
timeline.why: Measures how well a model briefs and checks subagents, which tests 1 and 2 cannot see.

timeline.title: GLM-5.3-Flash runs on Maya
timeline.what: Two engine patches lift decode from 4 to 19 tok/s; tests 1 and 2 both pass.
timeline.why: Can a large model work on one card?

timeline.title: Maker sampling and a loop guard
timeline.what: Entries serve the maker's recommended sampling, and the agent stops when it repeats itself.
timeline.why: Loops had ruined several runs.

timeline.title: Graders audited, all old runs regraded
timeline.what: 125 archived runs rechecked; four test-1 verdicts changed and some test counts were corrected.
timeline.why: Old and new scores must compare.

timeline.title: Old PCIe share doubles Flash-Next on Strata
timeline.what: Restoring the old PCIe share lifts long-answer decode from 48 to 95 tok/s.
timeline.why: A newer default had halved speed.

timeline.title: Test 4: ticket fixes in Rust
timeline.what: Tiel Coder fixed three tickets, three runs each, on a crate with 155 passing tests.
timeline.why: Tests 1 and 2 never touch existing code.

timeline.title: Engine shoot-out on Qwen3.8-27B
timeline.what: TensorFold, exllamav3 and llama.cpp compared with and without drafting on one 3090.
timeline.why: Pick the fastest stack for the daily model.

timeline.title: Tests 7 and 8 added
timeline.what: Test 7 is a seeded labyrinth generator; test 8 gives the pagoda and orrery to an agent.
timeline.why: Measure design work, not only code.

timeline.title: Agent window margin changed
timeline.what: At 150k served, the agent now compacts at 89,328 tokens (60%), up from 71,000 (47%).
timeline.why: Fewer compactions, longer runs.

timeline.title: Night search for speed at 141k context
timeline.what: Four stacks timed on code at 141k tokens; Gemma-4-26B-A4B kept 123 tok/s.
timeline.why: Find what stays fast with a long history.

timeline.title: Public model-research update; LFM2.5 and Saluki tested
timeline.what: LFM2.5-24B (five quants) and a 2-bit Qwen3.8-27B tune went through tests 1 and 2.
timeline.why: Check small and very low-bit models.

timeline.title: Strata 0.1.44.1, Maya 1.1.11, exllamav3 1.6.2
timeline.what: Strata cut load time and doubled decode in the A/B; Maya fixed split digits; exllamav3 matched.
timeline.why: Re-measure each engine before changing defaults.

timeline.title: First graded test 8 batches
timeline.what: Six models that drew blank one-shot pagodas scored 7 to 10 as agents.
timeline.why: Show what tools and a browser add.

timeline.title: llama.cpp 0.7.0 replaces 0.6.0 in the router
timeline.what: Version 0.7.0 adds a GPU cache for experts and an option to keep all experts in RAM.
timeline.why: Big mixture models need that cache.

timeline.title: Gyro-S quant on Strata 0.2
timeline.what: A 1-bit-class Flash-Next quant with an MTP draft decodes 119 tok/s and passes test 2 in 24 minutes.
timeline.why: Long agent runs at 20 tok/s are too slow.

timeline.title: Expert cache, Strata 0.2.2, Flint and tqLLM
timeline.what: Flash-Next sped up on llama.cpp and Strata; a new MoE and a new engine were tried.
timeline.why: Make the 125B model usable on one card.

timeline.title: Ornith 122B and Defiance pass tests 1 and 2
timeline.what: Ornith at 13.4 tok/s and Defiance at 32.5 tok/s both cleared the CLI checks and the Rust server tests.
timeline.why: Do the new large and uncensored quants finish a real task?

timeline.title: Heretic 2 passes the code tests
timeline.what: Five CLI checks, a 7-tool server with 34 passing tests, and three maintenance tickets. Both one-shots scored 0.
timeline.why: An abliterated Flash-Next quant had not been graded on this matrix.

timeline.title: A trust run whose tests did not compile
timeline.what: Orca uncensored passed test 1, plain test 2, and three test-4 tickets. Its trust run's tests failed to compile, so 0 and 0 is not a pass.
timeline.why: A green protocol line can hide a broken test build.

timeline.title: GPU unlock speeds long prefill
timeline.what: On our 3090 box, vLLM Qwen3.8-27B long-prompt prefill rose from 736 to about 1050 tok/s. Short decode stayed near 127 tok/s.
timeline.why: Does unlocking the GPU clock help a model that already fits on the card?

timeline.title: DeepSeek Maya-XS passes the agent tests
timeline.what: On Maya 1.1.28, both rounds passed tests 1, 2 and 3. Round 1 also passed the planted-docs run and all three test-4 tickets.
timeline.why: Can a DeepSeek flash pack do the agent work on one GPU?

timeline.title: DeepSeek one-shots, scored two ways in round 1
timeline.what: Round 1 is 7 of 10 and 10 of 10 on the final code block, and 0 on the harness packaging of the same replies. Round 2 is 9 of 10 and 10 of 10 on the file as delivered.
timeline.why: Does the picture hold when the reply is a single file?

timeline.title: DeepSeek keeps two sessions apart
timeline.what: UD-IQ1_S at 6 GPU layers decodes a 252k prompt at 3.09 tok/s. Nonce isolation was at about 8.8k tokens per session; 96k is the decode depth only.
timeline.why: A long cache has to survive a reload, and a second session must not leak into the first.

timeline.title: One graded round on the backlog
timeline.what: Tiel t06 7/8, Gemma on llama.cpp 2/8, OrcaSAQ 8/8, unpruned Flash-Next 8/8, Swift 6/8, Defiance 8/8, Qwopus 8/8 on two setups.
timeline.why: The public notes had stopped on 27 October.

timeline.title: Six Flash-Next quants, story draft only
timeline.what: Partial, one round, no hand grade. Draft decode runs from 28.8 to 104.2 tok/s. Two draft legs look anomalous. A second story round is queued for all six; rank none before it.
timeline.why: The edit speed is inflated by copying the draft.

timeline.title: Two cards: a 3090 and a V100
timeline.what: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash UD-IQ1_S spans both cards: 9.7 to 16.5 tok/s short-benchmark decode, 90k retrieval correct at 96k with the first token in 22 min (was 48.5). Qwopus 27B Q6_K runs on the V100 alone at 27 tok/s.
timeline.why: A second, larger card makes room for the expert cache and long context.

timeline.title: Unsloth v3.1 quants graded
timeline.what: Four quants, one round: all pass tests 3 and 4; UD-IQ1_M is fastest and draws best; one-shot pagodas all blank.
timeline.why: Alex expected the small quants to brute-force code but draw worse; the code half held, the art half did not.

timeline.title: Flash-Next toward 150 tok/s on one 3090
timeline.what: Strata 0.2.12: 98.8 to 128.6 tok/s short-benchmark decode (350 W, English draft vocabulary, stream draft-head norm, draft min-p 0.6); 120k prompts prefill at about 2,990 tok/s; adaptive fetch keeps decode at 124-127 tok/s right after a 120k prompt on the 3090 alone; four 128k slots with the V100 keep 109 tok/s per stream. Twenty more single-change runs did not beat it; UD-Q2_K_XL reaches 123.0 and UD-Q3_K_XL 112.0 on the same setup. A memory lock, Strata 0.2.13 and llamAmpere 0.6.3.8 changed nothing. On code and JSON the goal is met: a DFlash2 draft model on UD-Q2_K_XL gives 162 tok/s on code and 203 on JSON with the quality check passing; four streams together reach only about 125 tok/s on Strata, against 165 on llama.cpp; with a 3,072 MiB VRAM reserve four 30k slots (122.7 tok/s total) and two 100k slots (103.1 tok/s total) fit the 1.5 GiB rule.
timeline.why: Goal: 150 tok/s decode and 1,000+ tok/s prefill on a larger quant. Prefill is met; code and JSON decode are met; prose decode is at 86%, limited by the draft head.

timeline.title: Agent serving profile on one 3090
timeline.what: Two 256k slots with a 20k K/V window in VRAM and a host-RAM session cache: parked 155k sessions come back in 1.25 s, four 120k streams fit at 95.8 tok/s total, and two OpenCode agents ran at once with test 2 passing.
timeline.why: Alex wanted two large agent sessions served from the 3090 without re-reading long sessions on every switch.

lcpp-arete27b-q6k.note: Nous Research fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B. Fits the V100 alone, not the RTX 3090. Serving tuning is short-benchmark rates. Agent test 1 on the V100 alone (2026-11-10, Qwen thinking sampling): every live check passes, 11 subcommands, its own 59 tests pass, 60 minutes, 18.4 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.61 s. Agent test 2 (same setup): builds, 8 tools, the handshake and the tool call work, 48 of its own tests pass, 81 minutes at 20.7 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 1.11 s; 6.5 GiB free. The labyrinth (test 7, same setup, thinking on): A-C full marks (round trip, 10 of 10 distinct hidden-seed mazes, worst path 325 with 6 floor changes), D 1, E 1, total 8 of 10, in 4.4 hours at 21.0 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.61 s, 6.5 GiB free; the first dense 27B to take full A-C marks on the labyrinth, at about a sixth of Flash-Next's speed. Largest context on the V100 alone: 240k (1.0 GiB free, a 235k retrieval correct); 256k leaves 440 MiB, under our 512 MiB V100 floor.

lcpp-tiel35b-q6kxl-3090-v100.label: Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B UD-Q6_K_XL · llama.cpp (Clover 4838ffb), RTX 3090 + V100, 128k, 8-bit KV
lcpp-tiel35b-q6kxl-3090-v100.note: Serving tuning only: the whole Q6 model in VRAM across both cards (the V100 half empty). Short-benchmark rates. Agent test 1 (2026-11-10, thinking on, Qwen thinking sampling, OpenCode): it wrote eight files, then replied "Stopped." after 5 minutes as if interrupted (nothing interrupted it), with no entry point and no tests, so no live check could run; 103.5 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.15 s; 5.2 GiB free on the 3090. Agent test 1 again with thinking off (Qwen non-thinking sampling): every live check passes, 10 subcommands, 27 of its own tests pass, in 8 minutes at 98.3 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.31 s; 5.2 GiB free on the 3090. A small tool, but a working one. Agent test 2 with thinking off: the server does not build (9 errors left). At a 104k prompt the model wrote its next tool call as plain text instead of a real call, so the agent took it as a final answer and stopped after 11 minutes; 80.3 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.17 s. The labyrinth (test 7) with thinking off scored 0 of 10: after 28.6 hours it had handed in nothing (no generator, maze or notes). The conversation kept filling to about 107k tokens, OpenCode compacted it to about 7k about 80 times, and each time the model lost its progress on the maze design. We stopped it by hand; 82.0 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.44 s. A rerun of test 7 with OpenCode's dynamic context pruning plugin ended the compaction loop (13 prunes, no compactions) but still scored 0 of 10: after 2.5 hours the model wrote a file-write tool call as plain text and the session ended; 84.7 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.51 s. Test 2T with thinking off passes in 11 minutes: it builds, 6 tools, the handshake and the tool call work, 8 of its own tests pass, and it called only the real Home Assistant endpoints after testing the documented ones (82.1 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.52 s); a thin server that fought the compiler (187 Rust errors over 23 builds). On the V100 alone (short benchmark, thinking off) it fits 64k at 92 tok/s decode with a 60k retrieval correct and 1.5 GiB free, which leaves the 3090 free for another model.

strata0213-fnb-v31-udq2kxl-128k.label: Flash-Next UD-Q2_K_XL (Unsloth Dynamic v3.1) · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, 128k, 8-bit KV
strata0213-fnb-v31-udq2kxl-128k.note: Serving tuning toward 150 tok/s decode, then the daily driver (MTP draft head). Short-benchmark rates, except agent test 1 (2026-11-09): with engine-default sampling at 350 W, 120.6 tok/s agent-run decode but the CLI crashes on start; with Qwen thinking sampling at 300 W, 121.4 tok/s, first token median 0.37 s, every live check passes. Agent test 2 (Qwen thinking sampling, 300 W): full pass, 10 tools, its own 181 tests pass, 122.7 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.64 s. Test 2T, the variant with planted wrong notes (Qwen thinking sampling, 300 W): full pass, 8 tools, its own 120 tests pass, and it checked the notes against the live API before trusting them; 121.6 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.59 s. Test 7, the labyrinth: 9 of 10, 119.5 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.41 s.

strata0213-fnb-v31-udq3kxl-128k.label: Flash-Next UD-Q3_K_XL (Unsloth Dynamic v3.1) · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, 128k, 8-bit KV
strata0213-fnb-v31-udq3kxl-128k.note: Serving tuning toward 150 tok/s decode, short-benchmark rates; agent test 1 (2026-11-09, Qwen thinking sampling, 300 W): every live check passes, 17 subcommands, its own 298 tests pass, 106.8 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.36 s. Agent test 2: fail, the crate does not compile; after 12 minutes the agent called a tool OpenCode does not have and the session ended, 109.1 tok/s agent-run decode. Test 2T: full pass, 11 tools, its own 150 tests pass, notes checked against the live API, 108.5 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.67 s.

qwen3.8-flash-next-agent.label: Flash-Next UD-Q2_K_XL (Unsloth Dynamic v3.1) · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, agent profile: 2 × 256k slots, 8-bit KV, host-RAM session cache
qwen3.8-flash-next-agent.note: Agent serving profile (2026-11-10): the daily-driver quant with two 256k slots, 20,480 K/V cells per layer in VRAM and the rest in pinned host RAM, and a 28 GiB host-RAM session cache, one 3090 at 300 W. Agent test 2 run at the same time as a test 1 session on the same load (Qwen thinking sampling): full pass, 8 tools, its own 113 tests pass, 70 minutes, 39.2 tok/s agent-run decode per session (about 77 summed with the other session), first token median 1.36 s with prompts up to 217k tokens. The test 1 session beside it was cut by a test-harness thermal check, not graded.

strata0213-fnb-v31-udq20-128k.label: Flash-Next UD-Q2_0 (Unsloth Dynamic v3.1) · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, 128k, 8-bit KV
strata0213-fnb-v31-udq20-128k.note: The smaller 2-bit quant on the daily-driver setup (MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W), tried because smaller weights leave more expert-cache room in VRAM. Short-benchmark decode ties UD-Q2_K_XL (122.4 against 120.7 tok/s). Agent runs (2026-11-10, Qwen thinking sampling, OpenCode): test 1 passes with 471 of its own tests at 136.6 tok/s; test 2T passes with 9 tools and 85 tests at 137.0 tok/s and uses only the real endpoints; the labyrinth (test 7) scores 9 of 10 at 135.3 tok/s. First token median 0.25-0.39 s. Test 2 passes in full with 14 tools and 136 of its own tests at 137.8 tok/s (first token median 0.30 s), so it passes all four agent tests. On the agent serving profile (two 256k slots, two ~240k prompts at once, short benchmark) it decodes 104.3 tok/s total against 90.2 for UD-Q2_K_XL, with 3.1 GiB free. On the V100 as the only card (Strata 0.2.13 built for it, experts streamed from RAM), two 256k slots with all K/V on the card fit with 3.1 GiB free and hold two ~240k prompts at once (both needles correct), but the engine prefills one session at a time and turns drafting off for a session decoding beside a prefill: 31.7 tok/s for one drafted stream, 49.9 tok/s total. Across both cards (Strata 0.2.13, short benchmark, thinking on): eight 256k slots with 20k K/V cells per layer on the cards and the rest in pinned RAM hold eight ~240k prompts at once, all needles correct, 89.4 tok/s total and 9-15 tok/s per session, 2.5 GiB free on the 3090; four 256k slots with all K/V on the cards (layers split 24/24) hold four, all correct, 111.4 tok/s total, 3.2 GiB free. Prefill still runs one session at a time, so the eighth session waits about 20 minutes for its first token.

strata0213-fnb-gsq-iq3s-128k.label: Flash-Next GSQ-RCO IQ3_S · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, 128k, 8-bit KV
strata0213-fnb-gsq-iq3s-128k.note: A 3-bit quant rechecked on the daily-driver setup (MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W, Qwen thinking sampling), with only the weights changed from the UD-Q2_0 runs, to see whether more bits buy quality. Agent test 1 (2026-11-10, OpenCode): every live check passes, 20 subcommands, 255 of its own tests pass, 48 minutes at 117.2 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.31 s; 2.2 GiB free. Test 2: builds, 11 tools, the tool call works and 160 of its own tests pass (64 minutes, 118.0 tok/s, first token median 0.57 s), but it answers an initialize request for the 2024-11-05 protocol version with an error instead of offering a version it supports, so older clients cannot connect. The labyrinth (test 7) scores 8 of 10 at 118.0 tok/s (first token median 0.42 s): one fixed serpentine route for every seed. It is about 14% slower than UD-Q2_0 on every test and does not beat it on any.

strata0213-fnb-gsq-iq3xxs-128k.label: Flash-Next GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS · Strata 0.2.13, RTX 3090, 128k, 8-bit KV
strata0213-fnb-gsq-iq3xxs-128k.note: The smaller 3-bit GSQ quant on the daily-driver setup (MTP draft head, one 3090 at 300 W, Qwen thinking sampling), with only the weights changed from the UD-Q2_0 runs. Agent test 1 (2026-11-10, OpenCode): every live check passes, 18 subcommands, 263 of its own tests pass, 65 minutes at 128.9 tok/s agent-run decode, first token median 0.41 s; 2.2 GiB free. Test 2: builds, 9 tools, the 2024-11-05 handshake and the tool call work, 145 of its own tests pass (50 minutes, 134.3 tok/s, first token median 0.38 s). Faster than IQ3_S and close to UD-Q2_0, but fewer tools and tests than UD-Q2_0. The labyrinth (test 7) scored 8 of 10 at 129.2 tok/s (first token median 0.42 s): the route changes with each seed, but it is a comb of one-cell dead ends.

tf127-qwen3.8-27b-exl3-3bpw-dflash2.label: Qwen3.8-27B EXL3 3-bit · TensorFold 1.2.7, DFlash2 drafts, RTX 3090, 128k to 176k, 8-bit cache
tf127-qwen3.8-27b-exl3-3bpw-dflash2.note: The TensorFold 1.2.7 release archive, unchanged, on one 3090 at 300 W with an 8-bit (fp8) K/V cache. Short-benchmark rates. Drafted decode 79 to 87 tok/s on prose, 210 to 217 on code and 204 to 259 on JSON, first token 0.06 to 0.19 s on short prompts; 30k, 128k and 176k retrieval all correct (first token 41 s, 249 s and 388 s). Drafting is lossless here: all 15 fixed prompts give the same text with and without drafting, greedy and sampled, at 2.7 to 7.8 times the plain speed. Quality check 3 of 3. 3.6 GiB free at 176k, so it fits.

tf127-nemotron3.5-lightning-nvfp4.label: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B NVFP4 · TensorFold 1.2.7 (RTX 30 fallback path), RTX 3090, 32k
tf127-nemotron3.5-lightning-nvfp4.note: NVFP4 weights on a 3090, which has no FP4 hardware, through TensorFold's fallback path; it drafts with the export's own MTP head. Short-benchmark rates: 152 to 157 tok/s on prose and 181 to 194 on code, first token 0.04 s on short prompts; 30k retrieval correct with a 4.8 s first token (about 6,300 tok/s prefill). Quality check 1 of 3 (the code task passes; one wrong total and one answer in the wrong format), and we have no same-prompt run on another card to tell model from fallback arithmetic. 3.7 GiB free, fits.

lcpp-arete27b-q8.label: Arete-27B Q8_0 · llama.cpp (Clover 4838ffb), V100 alone, 128k, 8-bit KV
lcpp-arete27b-q8.note: The 8-bit quant of the Nous Research fine-tune, on the V100 alone. Serving tuning only (short-benchmark rates): 23.1 tok/s decode against 26.2 for Q6_K; 128k is the largest context that fits (a 120k retrieval correct, 0.9 GiB free). No agent tests yet.

lcpp-qwen38-27b-udq4km-3090.label: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_M (Unsloth, September 2026 file) · llama.cpp (Clover 4838ffb), RTX 3090, 96k, 8-bit KV
lcpp-qwen38-27b-udq4km-3090.note: The control for the Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 re-upload: the older file on the 3090 alone at 250 W. Short-benchmark rates: 32.1 tok/s decode, short-prompt first token 0.23-0.61 s, 30k and 90k retrievals correct, quality check 3 of 3, 5.4 GiB free. Agent test 1 with thinking on (agent run): passes all five checks with 94 tests passing, 8 subcommands, 68 minutes, engine decode 23.5 tok/s, median first token 0.38 s.

lcpp-qwen38-27b-v31-udq4km-3090.label: Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_M (Unsloth Dynamic V3.1) · llama.cpp (Clover 4838ffb), RTX 3090, 96k, 8-bit KV
lcpp-qwen38-27b-v31-udq4km-3090.note: Unsloth re-uploaded its Qwen3.8-27B quants as Dynamic V3.1 and claims 5-10% better agentic scores. Same flags as the old file, only the file changes. Short-benchmark rates: 32.3 tok/s decode (old file 32.1), short-prompt first token 0.21-0.61 s, 30k and 90k retrievals correct, quality check 3 of 3, 5.3 GiB free (94 MiB less than the old file). Agent test 1 with thinking on (agent run): passes all five checks with 58 tests passing, 7 subcommands, 57 minutes, engine decode 23.9 tok/s, median first token 0.41 s.
